readings.title: First reading
readings.text:
Thus says the Lord:
When Israel was a child I loved him,
and I called my son out of Egypt.
But the more I called to them, the further they went from me;
they have offered sacrifice to the Baals
and set their offerings smoking before the idols.
I myself taught Ephraim to walk,
I took them in my arms;
yet they have not understood that I was the one looking after them.
I led them with reins of kindness,
with leading-strings of love.
I was like someone who lifts an infant close against his cheek;
stooping down to him I gave him his food.
Ephraim, how could I part with you?
Israel, how could I give you up?
How could I treat you like Admah,
or deal with you like Zeboiim?
My heart recoils from it,
my whole being trembles at the thought.
I will not give rein to my fierce anger,
I will not destroy Ephraim again,
for I am God, not man:
I am the Holy One in your midst
and have no wish to destroy.

exegesis.summary: Through the prophet Hosea, God speaks with the tenderness of a father who taught his little one to walk, lifting Israel to his cheek and bending down to feed him. Though Israel has run to idols, God refuses to unleash his fierce anger, for he is God and not man—the Holy One in the midst of his people. This oracle is one of the most maternal, paternal, and self-revealing passages of the Old Testament, disclosing a God whose mercy overcomes his just wrath.

patristicQuotes.quote: The Lord, who keepeth not His anger for ever, remembered the woes He had brought upon Egypt, and therefore sent His Son thither, and gives it this sign of great reconciliation, that with this one remedy He might heal the ten plagues of Egypt, and the nation that had been the persecutor of this first-born people, might be the guardian of His first-born Son.

Ephraim signifies fertility... When the elder people were forgotten and passed over, there came an abundant harvest from the Gentiles. Our Lord left the Jews, and went forth into a country—the whole world—near the wilderness, the deserted Church, to Ephraim, the fruitful city; and there continues with His disciples up to this day.

cccReferences.title: God, merciful and gracious, slow to anger
God faithful to the fathers, compassionate to their descendants
Moses stands in the breach: God cannot forsake his people

exegesis.thematicConnection: The Father's cry, 'I called my son out of Egypt,' is quoted by Matthew of the infant Christ, and today's Gospel shows this same tender Father sending out the Twelve gratuitously, because his kingdom flows from mercy freely given, not earned.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
Let your face shine on us, O Lord, and we shall be saved.
O shepherd of Israel, hear us,
shine forth from your cherubim throne.
O Lord, rouse up your might,
O Lord, come to our help.
Let your face shine on us, O Lord, and we shall be saved.
God of hosts, turn again, we implore,
look down from heaven and see.
Visit this vine and protect it,
the vine your right hand has planted.
Let your face shine on us, O Lord, and we shall be saved.
readings.refrain: Let your face shine on us, O Lord, and we shall be saved.

exegesis.summary: Israel, chastened and scattered, begs the Shepherd enthroned upon the cherubim to shine forth and save his vine. The refrain—'Let your face shine on us, O Lord'—is the very prayer Hosea's God is longing to answer. The psalm confesses that salvation is not something Israel can achieve; it comes when the Lord himself visits, looks down, and protects the vineyard he planted.

patristicQuotes.quote: By these words, Before the face, he signifies that our Lord's incarnation would be visible to all men. And this salvation he says is to be the light of the Gentiles and the glory of Israel.

cccReferences.title: Our restless heart seeks the face of God
The Church's cry of hope amid trial

exegesis.thematicConnection: The vine God tenderly planted is the same 'son' he called from Egypt in Hosea. In the Gospel, the shining face of the Shepherd draws near in the mission of the Twelve, who visit the vine bringing healing and the nearness of the Kingdom.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text: Jesus instructed the Twelve as follows: ‘As you go, proclaim that the kingdom of heaven is close at hand. Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out devils. You received without charge, give without charge. Provide yourselves with no gold or silver, not even with a few coppers for your purses, with no haversack for the journey or spare tunic or footwear or a staff, for the workman deserves his keep.

exegesis.summary: Jesus commissions the Twelve with the same fatherly heart Hosea revealed: 'You received without charge, give without charge.' The Kingdom is near because the Father's mercy has drawn near in Christ, and now he entrusts that mercy to apostolic hands that must remain empty of gold, silver, and every self-reliance. Their poverty is the credential of the gift they carry.

patristicQuotes.quote: A happy exchange! In place of gold and silver, and the like, they received power to heal the sick, to raise the dead... He made them Angels more than men, freeing them from all anxiety of this life, that they might have but one care, that of teaching... nothing is so pleasant as to be delivered from all care and anxiety, God being present, and being to us instead of all things.
Because the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the profit of the Church, after bestowing His power on the Apostles, He sends them that they may exercise this power for the good of others.

cccReferences.title: The Twelve share in Christ's authority and mission
The Twelve as foundation of the new Israel
Detachment from riches for the sake of the Kingdom

exegesis.thematicConnection: The apostles embody Hosea's God: they go stooping down to lift up the sick, the possessed, and the dead, as the Father once stooped to feed Ephraim. Freely they have received the shining face of the Shepherd; freely they now give it.

synthesis.title: Freely you have received: the tender God who stoops to save
synthesis.body: Today the Church places before us the most vulnerable face of God. In Hosea, the Almighty speaks not as a distant judge but as a father who taught his child to walk, held him against his cheek, and now cannot bring himself to destroy: 'I am God, not man; the Holy One in your midst.' This is the mystery of divine mercy that outstrips human wrath. The Psalm receives this revelation as prayer: shepherd of Israel, shine forth, visit this vine you planted, let your face shine on us. What Israel begs, the Father accomplishes by sending his Son—the true Son called out of Egypt—and by extending that mission through the Twelve. In the Gospel, Jesus commissions them to proclaim that the Kingdom is 'close at hand,' precisely because the tender nearness Hosea foretold has arrived in person. Their poverty—no gold, no silver, no spare tunic—is not asceticism for its own sake but the sign that everything they carry is pure gift: 'You received without charge, give without charge.' The Church today invites us to recognize that we ourselves are the Ephraim God refuses to abandon, the vine he keeps visiting, and, if we have been baptized, the sent ones through whom his face still shines upon a world hungering to be lifted to the Father's cheek.
